title: Given an array of bar heights representing a histogram where each bar has width 1, find the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely within the histogram.
shortTitle: Largest Rectangle in Histogram: increasing stack, compute area on pop
keyPoints: Use an increasing monotonic stack of indices; when a shorter bar arrives, pop each taller bar and compute its maximal rectangle.
The width of a popped bar's rectangle is currentIndex minus the new stack top minus 1; if the stack is empty, the width is currentIndex.
Append a virtual bar of height 0 at the end to flush all remaining bars from the stack without a separate cleanup loop.
The increasing stack guarantees that the element below a popped bar is its nearest shorter bar on the left.
Time is O(n) because each index is pushed and popped exactly once; space is O(n) for the stack.
Use a long accumulator for area to avoid integer overflow on large inputs.

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep an increasing stack of indices; when a shorter bar arrives, pop each taller bar and compute its rectangle using the width between the new top and the current index.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Largest Rectangle in Histogram** – find the area of the biggest rectangle fitting under a histogram of unit-width bars.
- **Increasing monotonic stack** – hold indices whose heights increase from bottom to top, so each bar's nearest shorter neighbor on the left is the bar below it on the stack.
- **Area on pop** – when a shorter bar triggers a pop, the rectangle height is the popped bar's height and the width stretches from the new stack top to the current index.
- **Sentinel trick** – append a virtual bar of height 0 to force every real bar off the stack.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time and O(n) space; each index enters and leaves the stack once.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya at National Bank of India looks at a bar chart of daily trading volumes and wants the biggest solid rectangle she can draw inside it. For each bar she asks: how far left and right can I extend while staying at least this tall? She keeps a pile of bars still growing taller. When a shorter bar appears, every taller bar on the pile can no longer extend rightward, so she pops each and measures its rectangle. The biggest one across all bars is the answer.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Largest Rectangle in Histogram uses an increasing monotonic stack to find, in one linear pass, the widest span over which each bar is the shortest. When a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar on the stack can no longer extend rightward, so I pop each and compute its rectangle. The height is the popped bar's height, and the width stretches from the new stack top to the current index.

The increasing stack guarantees that the bar below a popped bar is the nearest shorter bar on its left, and the current bar that triggered the pop is the nearest shorter bar on its right. Those two boundaries define the maximal rectangle for the popped bar. I use the sentinel trick of appending a virtual height-0 bar at the end to flush all remaining bars without a separate cleanup loop.

The complexity is O(n) because each index is pushed and popped exactly once. The width formula, `i - stack.peek() - 1`, is the source of the most common off-by-one mistake, and the empty-stack guard that uses width `i` instead is essential when the popped bar extends all the way to the left edge. For large inputs I use a `long` accumulator to avoid integer overflow.

In my project at the National Bank of India, I applied this to a histogram of hourly trading volumes to find the largest sustained-volume block. The quadratic brute force was too slow over a full trading session, and the increasing stack gave both boundaries for each bar in a single linear pass, making the analytics dashboard responsive even on months of hourly data.

Remember one sentence: keep an increasing stack of indices, compute area on every pop using width from the new top to the current index, and the sentinel flushes all remaining bars.
